extracted.intended_audience: student journalists and beginning reporters (high-school and college newspaper staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing news leads and follow-up stories, focusing on which element to emphasize in a story and on grammatical ways to begin a lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playing up an element
rubrics_metrics.description: To play up an element in a news story is to make that element, rather than other elements, significant. The significant goes into the first line of the lead of a news article. The element played up need not be the main event; it may be some fact, or condition, or contingency accompanying the main event or contained in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide what to emphasize based on the interests of the paper's subscribers. Examples: play up Hunt’s daring in a chess tournament rather than his loss; for a dull football game, play up the good-natured crowds. The element played up becomes the 'peak' that gives unity to the account; other elements revolve about it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select the element based on reader interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Interests of the subscribers to the paper must largely determine what should be played up in an article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To justify including outside/world news in a high school paper, make a point of contact between that news and the special interests of the student body. Choose the element most likely to catch the reader’s interest; adapt emphasis for different reader classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playing-up device secures unity and prevents monotony
rubrics_metrics.description: The device of playing up an element, besides challenging the interest of the reader, secures unity in the account and prevents dead-level monotony in narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the emphasized element as the 'peak' of the mountain range: it identifies the story and prevents cataloguing; use for reports of dinners, parades, exhibitions, awards, and similar items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize significance, avoid sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: At all times what is significant, not what is sensational, should be played up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid emphasizing sensational elements (yellow journalism). The chosen emphasis should be significant to readers rather than merely sensational.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use the playing-up device (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The playing-up device is valuable in: 1. Reporting exhibitions, dinners, awards, and the like. 2. Adapting news to the immediate interests of the student body. 3. Bringing world-wide news into the high school paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three application areas as practical tests for when to center a story on a single element.

rubrics_metrics.name: After choosing the element, consider grammatical beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: Having decided on the most interesting part of the story to put into the lead concretely, the journalist should consider the grammatical form of his beginning. Variety of beginning is to be aimed at on a page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong, varied beginning helps avoid monotony; 'Briskly Begun Is Half Done.' The grammatical form of the lead should match the element you are playing up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ten grammatical ways to begin
rubrics_metrics.description: The ten ways to begin (order based on frequency in several issues of the New York Times): 1. Noun 2. Prepositional phrase 3. Participle 4. Noun clause 5. Infinitive 6. Cause clause 7. Concession clause 8. Conditional clause 9. Nominative absolute 10. Time clause
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these ten forms as a menu for lead openings; vary openings across a page. The order reflects common usage frequency but choose form by effect you want.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noun beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: Noun.—Omit The, An or A unless there is no other way to begin. Never begin with figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a concrete noun to foreground the subject or object; do not start leads with numerals. Examples in text show how noun leads establish topic immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepositional phrase beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepositional phrase.—To play up circumstances attending an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a prepositional phrase when you want to foreground setting, time, or other circumstances (e.g., 'PARIS, July 26—Amid exquisite settings...'). Use it to set scene or context for the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participle / participial phrase beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: Participle.—To play up action attending the main verb rather than the actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use present participles to emphasize ongoing action (e.g., 'Finishing in a whirlwind attack...') or past participles for states ('Given the right of way...'). Beware of dangling participles; ensure the participial phrase clearly modifies the subject of the main clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noun-clause beginning (that/how/why/what/whether)
rubrics_metrics.description: Noun.—Noun clause beginning with that, how, why, what, whether.—To play up a summary of a result, opinion, or statement, used as subject of the main verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with 'That', 'How', 'Why', 'What', or 'Whether' to foreground a conclusion, opinion, or central issue (e.g., 'That the low point... has been reached is indicated by reports...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitive beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinitive.—To play up action as the subject of the main verb; to play up purpose. (Order that is not used in journalism.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with 'To' + verb when you want to treat an action or purpose as the grammatical subject (e.g., 'To cleanse the world of leprosy... is the aim...'). Use sparingly and deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clause-of-cause beginning (because/since/as)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clause of cause beginning with because, since, as.—To play up cause or motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cause clauses to foreground motive or reason (e.g., 'Because the Sioux Tribe... a new form of Indian warfare is likely...'). Note: this construction should not be used too often.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concession clause beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: Concession clause.—Listed as one of the grammatical ways to begin (number 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a concession clause (e.g., beginning with 'Although' or 'Even though') to acknowledge a counterpoint while foregrounding the main fact; examples and extended guidance appear elsewhere in the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional clause beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditional clause.—Listed as one of the grammatical ways to begin (number 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a conditional clause (e.g., 'If...') when the story’s significance or outcome depends on a condition; choose this when the conditional relationship is central to the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominative absolute beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominative absolute.—Listed as one of the grammatical ways to begin (number 9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a nominative absolute construction to add a detached phrase that sets circumstance (e.g., 'The meeting concluded, the committee...'). Employ for variety and to compactly state a circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-clause beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: Time clause.—Listed as one of the grammatical ways to begin (number 10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a time clause (e.g., 'When...', 'While...', 'As...') to place the action in temporal context and to emphasize timing as the key element of the lead.
